author: Trip.com Member
text: Everything about this hotel was great. I especially loved the breakfast — it was delicious and a perfect start to the day. A huge thank you to the super friendly staff who made me feel so welcome. The location is also a major plus, as it’s close to everything. I will definitely be back!

author: joules w
text: Possibly the best hotel I've ever been to. Super friendly and helpful staff, and seriously the best breakfast buffet full of fresh fruit and juices, eggs, sausages, pastries and even sushi. There is a big gym, nature trails with free roaming tortoises, and a few delicious restaurants as well. Love the old sitting rooms too. Couldn't be happier.

author: Megan Skye
text: It was such an incredible experience. The mountains are gorgeous. The gardens are beautiful. The staff is incredibly friendly and professional. The outside restaurant for breakfast and lunch has the most beautiful Mountain views. The food is delicious. The breakfast buffet is the best breakfast selection I’ve seen and tasted, I’ve travelled all over the world and nothing beats Vineyard hotel. The beds are so comfy. The gym is luxurious and quiet with the most beautiful Mountain View’s. Our room view was beautiful too. I loved everything about this place. I’ll definitely be back. Highly recommend.

author: Meera Hoosen
text: Beautiful afternoon high tea at the Vineyard Hotel with friends. The setting is peaceful and scenic, with magnificent mountain views and well-kept gardens that make you slow down and appreciate the surroundings. The high tea was enjoyable, the scones were fresh, and the atmosphere relaxed and welcoming. Service was attentive without being intrusive. One of the highlights was seeing the resident tortoise quietly moving through the gardens — such a lovely unexpected moment. A very pleasant Cape Town experience overall.”

author: L O
text: Dropped in for Breakfast, Now I've had the pleasure to visit Hotels & Restaurants from all around the world and this place was such a refreshing surprise. The quality and combination of food for Brunch was exceptional, the staff was unmatched in their attentiveness and friendliness. Totally mind blown, what an excellent spot, Will be coming back soon. Thank You All 😇🙌🏼

author: Jayesh Tailor
text: The Vineyard, is rated as a 4star Hotel but I rate The Vineyard as a 5 Star. I have stayed at The Vineyard many times, sometimes two or three times a year. Most hotels have comfortable beds, showers, baths, tv, kettle, iron, swimming pool, gym etc etc. However what other hotels do not have is the exceptional and wonderful staff that The Vineyard has. Each and every staff member goes above and beyond to deliver exceptional service and care for all visitors to the hotel not just the guests. The staff are hard working, attentive, helpful, forward thinking, caring, understanding. During my work or my travels if things go wrong, yes I will complain but if my complaint is due to bad service then I always blame management for not providing adequate training and for The Vineyard I compliment not only staff but the management also, for getting the training of their staff to such a perfection. We had the pleasure of being served at the restaurants by many people but one person will always be in my memory. Trust, one of the waiters in the courtyard restaurant, we were a group of 7, Trust was perfect in his service and care for all the guests. What stood out about Trust was that 10 minutes or so after we all left the table, I went back to my room and I received a phone call, I did not hear very well, but I heard something like “on the table” and I said to Trust “ I will come down” I figured that I may have left my my hand sanitiser on the table. When I got to the restaurant Trust came out from the kitchen holding some money, “sir you left this on the table” I had completely forgotten I had left 400Rand on the table! It would be totally understandable if Trust had thought this was an additional tip and 99% people would think that but not Trust he called to tell me and safely kept the money until I came down. 400Rand is not a lot of money in the grand scheme of things but it is the principal which Trust adheres to, honesty and he lives by his name, Trust! Thank You Trust Thank You The Vineyard. See you again soon

author: Fazlyn Petersen
text: The ambience and scenery at the restaurant was lovely. The desserts looked beautiful but I didn't enjoy them. My sundae had liquid at the bottom when it arrived at my table. It wasn't very hot so I didn't expect it to be melted when it arrived. I was told that it happens. I asked them replaced it with cheesecake. The cheesecake was more yellow than expected and average. My friend's carrot cake and scones were more enjoyable.

author: Cece Kearns
text: Had such a lovely lunch at The Vineyard Hotel. The setting is absolutely beautiful, with peaceful gardens and stunning mountain views that make the whole experience feel so relaxing. The food was delicious, beautifully presented, and the service was warm and attentive throughout. The atmosphere was calm, elegant, and perfect for a lunch date. Definitely one of those places that makes you want to come back again. Highly recommend for anyone looking for a beautiful lunch spot in Cape Town.

author: holly kidd
text: I recently stayed at The Vineyard for my 40th bday weekend. I was drawn to it from the gorgeous photos of the garden on the website. It did not disappoint. The hotel was such a welcoming, uber lush and comfortable place for my first visit to South Africa. Walking around the gardens under the table mountain, after a lavish breakfast, and meeting some resident tortoises was a highlight. Would have loved a swim if the weather had been warmer or a sauna if there was one. I particularly loved the Holly tree, see if you can find it :) The staff went extra miles and were happy to serve our requests. Thanks for the special memories.

author: Thais
text: It was a very pleasant experience staying at this hotel. It’s in a perfect location to experience the vibrant Cape Town Waterfront, surrounded by excellent places to eat, drink, and shop. The rooms are spacious and comfortable, with good mountain and harbor views if you choose the Mountain Facing rooms. We found the staff at reception, the restaurant, and the valet parking to be particularly friendly. They have a beautifully designed restaurant with a wonderful terrace for enjoying breakfast. If I had to find a fault, I didn’t quite understand the breakfast included with extras for basic items like coffee and eggs, but it doesn’t represent an exorbitant cost. You can enjoy the pool, spa, and gym at the nearby Queen Victoria Hotel. In short, a very good option for accommodation in this charming city.

author: Trip.com Member
text: The duty Manager, Victoria, was great and very accommodating. It was our wedding anniversary and Victoria accommodated our request for a view facing Table Mountain. We were very happy about that. The housekeeping staff were brilliant, always smiling and joyful to all guests making them feel welcome. In terms of the restaurant/breakfast area, it was quite disappointing as we noticed some guests receiving more attention than others, and at times, felt as though we were ignored and invisible. Unfortunately, on our last day, we bit into a sharp and hard piece of what seemed like bottle plastic in the food from the buffet section. When alerting the restaurant staff, they did not really seem bothered about the danger it had should we have swallowed it.

author: Trek28439570452
text: Totally recommended; great service, a peaceful atmosphere, and exceptionally helpful staff throughout the hotel. The in-house restaurant, Ginja, was outstanding, offering both excellent quality and a wide variety of yummy food, matched by warm and attentive service.||A special shout-out to Ayah, who truly made our experience memorable. As our server, he went above and beyond to make our group feel completely at home. Every request was handled quickly and thoughtfully, often improved by his suggestions and genuine kindness. Everyone at our table was commenting on how fantastic he was and how tasty the food was. ||We will definitely be returning to this hotel in the future!

author: 603janetv
text: Fabulous hotel that has managed to maintain the charm of a bygone era with a modern, crisp and comfortable atmosphere. The staff are friendly and accommodating. The food is excellent!! Breakfast consists of a bountiful spread and ala carte is also available. Overlooking Table Mountain, the views from the restaurant are breathtaking. With sufficient indoor and outdoor seating there are enough spots to choose from.

author: Stephanie Brumbaugh
text: We absolutely loved our stay at the Victoria & Alfred Hotel in Cape Town! The location is fantastic and made it so easy to explore the area on foot. Being able to walk to so many shops, restaurants, and attractions was such a huge plus. The views from the hotel are incredible and made every moment feel special. Waking up to that scenery each day was unforgettable. The breakfast was also top tier - delicious, plentiful, and the perfect way to start the day. Everything about our stay was wonderful, and we’re already looking forward to coming back. Highly recommend!

author: lynnpS6421FD
text: We have just left this large but cosy hotel. We had a loft room on the 3rd floor which was unusual, clean, warm, had everything you needed. The sloping windows are a feature but I would have liked to be able to see more out of them - they have narrow shutters. But that was my only complaint. |The staff were helpful and pleasant, food in the restaurant was reasonably priced and well presented. |Breakfast was a pleasure too. |The waterfront location is fantastic, you really should stay here.

author: Kayla Thomas
text: We stayed here during our honeymoon (September 2025), and everything about our experience was absolutely wonderful! The hotel is beautiful, and the staff were some of the friendliest and kindest people we met on our trip. I wish I could remember the names of our breakfast servers because they were all so amazing and welcoming each morning. The buffet and hot breakfast (and the coffee!) were SO good—definitely one of the highlights of our stay. We also had dinner at the hotel restaurant one night, and it was honestly one of the best steaks I’ve ever had. Every meal felt special and perfectly prepared. The location couldn’t have been better—it’s right on the waterfront, within easy walking distance to shops, restaurants, and the main area where you can catch the hop-on hop-off bus. Our room was huge, spotless, and surprisingly quiet despite facing the main waterfront area. We were also greeted with a bottle of sparkling wine and chocolates, which was such a thoughtful and sweet touch. Everything about this hotel exceeded our expectations. It was the perfect place to stay in Cape Town, and we’d absolutely stay here again in a heartbeat!

author: MsG_13
text: This was the first stop on a much longer holiday for me. The hotel is in a great location, with shopping and eateries all round. ||Our room was big, very clean and comfortable with everything you would expect to have in the room. Our room overlooked the shopping side and was a bit noisy sometimes, but we were out a lot so this wasn't something we would have requested a room change for.||We had breakfast every morning at the dockside with fantastic views of Table Mountain. We also had dinner there once as enjoyed the food.||Also a good location for tour pickups. We walked to get the ferry for Robben Island.

author: Andy Meighen
text: Well you could not get any more central than this. Right on the waterfront. Rooms were fine. I liked the big pillows, but the mattress was quite bouncy! Service was great and breakfast choices excellent. We stayed four nights and two mornings the cooked breakfasts took a long time. The other two were quick. It was a bit of pot luck

author: Andrew Morgan
text: A perfect choice overlooking the harbour and a stunning view of table top mountain from the restaurant and patio. Ideal position to explore Cape Town and the great restaurants and tourist attractions etc in the V&A waterfront area. Lovey breakfast and staff. Large chic studio room. Would recommend Table Top mountain visit on the tour bus, Robben Island Tour and The Cape Peninsula Tour. We loved Cape Town.

author: Shawn Page
text: Our stay at Nsala was fantastic. From the moment we arrived we encountered tons of animals. Our guide Sunday was exceptional and gave us some incredible experiences. We saw all the animals (Lions, Leopard, Rhinos, Elephants, Giraffes, etc.) and had some incredible up close encounters. The service staff was up to par with our guide and gave us delicious meals & clean spaces the entire time we were there. Matthew our host had amazing hospitality, and went the extra mile to make sure we had a great time. I would recommend this place to anyone looking for a Safari in the area it does not disappoint.

author: Johnathan Page
text: I had a wonderful experience at Nsala. Our guide Sunday did an amazing job. We saw lions, wild dogs, a leopard, elephants, rhinos and so much more. The accommodations, service staff, and food were top notch. Lastly; the owner, Mathew, went above and beyond to make sure our experience was excellent. I highly recommend.

author: Milad Jokari
text: We had a wonderful stay at Nsala Wilderness Camp. The staff, Sunday, Vikie, Aron, and Girlie are truly warm and welcoming, and Cecil is a fantastic addition to the team. Every moment of our four-day stay was memorable. We were fortunate enough to spot four of the Big Five, along with many other animals. While wildlife sightings always involve luck and nothing is guaranteed, Sunday is an excellent tracker and led us to some truly spectacular wildlife encounters. Cecil’s presence also added greatly to our overall experience and enjoyment of the stay. A big thank you to the entire team, and to Matthew, for organizing such an outstanding lodge and safari experience. Regarding the camp itself, there are two daily game drives—one early in the morning at 5 and another in the afternoon at 4. In between, there is plenty of time to relax, enjoy delicious meals, and take in the beautiful surroundings. Wildlife can often be seen passing by or even through the camp. Despite occasional close encounters with hyenas, we always felt completely safe thanks to the attentive and professional staff who were always nearby. We are grateful for the experience and plan to visit Nsala again in future

author: Vasile Casco
text: We had an absolutely unforgettable stay at Nsala Wilderness Camp! 🌿 From the moment we arrived, we felt completely immersed in nature — with animals casually visiting us throughout the day. The lodge is intimate (max 10 guests), so even if it’s full, you get a personal, homey atmosphere. We were lucky enough to be the only guests during our stay, so it felt like VIP treatment from start to finish. The staff is outstanding. Sunday, our ranger, was incredibly respectful, friendly, and truly skilled — it was our very first safari and we were amazed to see all of the Big 5! Shana made us feel right at home and gave us great tips throughout our stay, while James impressed us with his amazing cooking skills. Big thanks also to everyone else who worked behind the scenes to make everything perfect. The lodge itself is comfortable and beautifully designed in true safari style — the perfect place to relax, disconnect, and soak in the wilderness. We loved the great conversations and drinks by the campfire, and enjoyed good coffee while watching the sunrise and getting ready for the impressive game drives that followed. This trip exceeded all expectations. Highly recommended for anyone looking for an intimate, authentic, and unforgettable safari experience! 🌅🦁🐘

author: Arres Oudshoorn
text: We've had a great time at this camp during our 3-day stay. The onsite staff is super friendly. Vision prepares tasty meals which were very welcome after game drives where the ranger really went the extra mile for a unique experience (saw 4/5 of the big five, including 2 up-close Leopard sightings and an up-close Rhino sighting). There is ample time to re-charge in between game drives in your room or at the swimming pool next to the wildlife that frequents the camp (such as hyenas and monkeys).

author: Suman Mampilly
text: Sunday, Aaron, and Vickie were amazing and took such good care of us the entire time we were there! Not to mention Sunday's patience and determination while we were on safari rides. Truly one of the best experiences we had in South Africa!!

author: Laura Brockie
text: We just spent 4 nights at Nsala and had an unforgettable time! Though nervous initially after reading some recent poor reviews, this was far from our experience. The lodge is beautiful, clean, and peaceful. We also never had any issues with power or internet. It was particularly lovely to sit on the deck watching zebra, warthog, and incredible bird life pass by. Vision is a fabulous chef and every meal was delicious! Our experience was made though by our fantastic and knowledgeable game driver, Shoas. He put in the extra mile and we loved his off piece expeditions to get close up to the animals. Due to some unforeseen wind our game viewings were reduced over the last couple of days, but we were so pleased with our other encounters (including 4 of the big 5, and 2 leopard sightings)! Thank you Nsala!

author: Vanessa B
text: Our stay at Nsala Wilderness Camp was incredible! The camp is beautifully integrated into the bush, offering comfort and stunning views. The staff were welcoming and knowledgeable, making every game drive an adventure—we saw lions, elephants, and even a leopard!

author: Maryke Rademeyer
text: Spent a lovely couple of nights at Nsala, where we were booked after well by the entire team there, including the resident mongoose family, monkeys and hyena. The view of the bush from the deck and the pool provided many opportunities to view elephants as they passed by the lodge, with the game drives delivering in some beautiful sightings. Thank you to everyone at Nsala for making our time there so special.

author: Patricia López Díaz
text: Nsala Camp was an absolutely lovely lodge. We had a great experience in this place thanks to our tour Sunday. He is a very experienced and nice man who shows you all the special areas where you can find animals in the Safari. We are still in contact with him, we are friends! The food was unreal very fresh and healthy! We will have an unforgettable memory of our honeymoon thanks to Sunday and all his team. Patricia Lopez Diaz y Gary Lynch

author: Julian John
text: Really awesome Hotel and conference facilities. Service is great from the Security, all the way to the entrance, front desk and catering staff. I must say the Security were so friendly and helpful, showing me where to park then escorting me to the reception. The hotel is really plush and luxurious. The food was amazing - from the pastries/snack food to the full lunch. Conference facilities were great. In fact there was no glitch at all during the entire conference. Great venue overall

author: NortonerStratford
text: We had an absolutely superb stay here. We often travel from the UK, our usual hotel was not available so we booked the Houghton.....what a great find!||We were upgraded from a studio to a city view room. The room was enormous, with everything we needed.||I had a spa treatment which was excellent. We used the indoor and outdoor pools and steam room, all of which were clean and modern. ||The food was excellent, lots of choice and beautifully cooked. We had cocktails in the bar and sat around the terrace with our sushi.||The thing that makes the hotel is the staff. From the gentleman who checks you into the car park, the waiting staff to the management, all were lovely and made us feel totally welcome. ||The hotel is safe with secure parking and shopping and restaurant areas nearby. We will definitely be back.

author: Trip.com Member
text: Nice localtion.Very friendly the staff

author: Brad Morehead
text: Great experience with the staff. Wonderful room and food and view of the city. Would definitely come back. We had a brief snafu with the reservation, but the team resolved it and everything was great. The food for dinner was excellent.

author: Lesanne Dunlop
text: I would just like to say that the Houghton hotel has one of the most outstanding customer service teams I have ever encountered. I left my phone in an uber, the driver was not getting back to me and seemingly had no intention of returning it. Their security team, specifically Gordon and Mark as well as the houghton driver, drove an hour away to a sketchy part of Johannesburg at night to retrieve my phone from this driver! I was leaving the country early the next morning so without them would not have been able to get my phone back. I just can not thank you guys enough for your efforts and real sincerity in wanting to help me. You truly went ABOVE and BEYOND! Thank you thank you thank you! 🙏 Aside from this amazing service, the rest of the team were just so wonderful the entire time we were there. The food was great, the spa was amazing, the rooms were lovely. We will MOST definitely be coming back. Thank you again guys! 🙏🙏🙏

author: Lwazi Radebe
text: Its a bit difficult to rate here because i only went there for a summit at one of their events/conference rooms. With being said, the security from the moment you enter the boom, they are very welcoming and thorough. The room was neat, good sound and visuals setup. Nothing negative to note really. The staff showing me where to go were great.

author: travelnicolle
text: We spent our final night in South Africa at The Houghton, staying in a two-bedroom penthouse with a private pool and jacuzzi. It was truly spectacular, easily the most expansive suite we have ever experienced. While the hardware of the hotel is stunning, the service is what defines the stay. From the lovely front desk and luggage team who greeted us with champagne, to the seamless hospitality after check-out, we felt completely looked after. They stored our luggage and gave us full access to the pool for the day, even providing private bathroom facilities to freshen up before our international flight. A world-class experience from start to finish.

author: Abdul Kader Mohamed
text: I recently had the opportunity to visit the Hotel for a business lunch. I was pleasantly surprised by the beauty and decor - it made me feel like, for a moment i was outside Johannesburg and in some international/cosmopolitan city. For a moment I felt like some important person, enjoying the good things in life. The food and service did not disappoint and just added to the experience. Good vibe. Good food. Good service. Real lifestyle!

author: Zeenat harper-valentine
text: Hotel and staff was absolutely stunning! My issue is with the restaurant and staff -Nova Bistro. There was a menu special - 2 course and 3 course. Offered freely last week and we thoroughly enjoyed it. I brought my sister and brother in law today and was refused this menu...citing it was incorrectly used. I booked my dining experience in advance and was thoroughly disappointed. Nobody called to inform me of this change -had they done so, I wouldn't have traveled all this way to enjoy the meal. Disappointed is an understatement and because of this...I will not return and do not endorse this restaurant. Staff are arrogant and have no idea how to put the customer first. I was then told to reserve my table on dining city...which I tried and was not allowed. The staff then informed me that the menu is now only allowed for during the week. Absolute joke...last time here for sure

author: MarkR-Sheffield
text: Our first stay at the Houghton and won’t be our last. After 24 hours of travelling with an overnight flight from the UK, we arrived tired at 9 am. Without asking, we are offered a suite as a day room until our room was ready. This gave us a chance for a couple of hours sleep and freshen up, and was genuinely highly appreciated. ||||our room was larger than expected, with a fab bathroom. ||||The lunchtime restaurant on the outside terrace presented 2 wonderful salads, but the highlight of our 2 night stay was dinner at Cyra which is worthy of a Michelin star, with some highly innovative dishes, all exquisitely presented. It is no surprise that in the 12 months it’s been open It’s won many awards for Chef Candice, who delightfully came out and introduced herself. ||||The customer service is excellent. As we were checking out and waiting for our taxi, one of their senior staff noticed my wife who was poorly that morning & immediately sat with her and ordered a coke to help settle her upset stomach. ||||As golfers, we played the Houghton course, which although we found it quite challenging being long with plenty of water hazards - most beautifully presented and I am not surprised that it is hosting the DP World Tour Joburg Open in 2026. ||||Personally, I rate this hotel very highly,

author: Avinash das
text: I recently stayed at Pavilion Hotel in Durban and unfortunately had a disappointing experience during my visit. I was allocated Room 124, which is located directly in front of the store room area. The room door lock was not functioning properly, and I was informed by the staff that the battery was down. Each time I required assistance, I had to personally go down to the reception for support. Additionally, the television and room telephone were not working during my stay, which made communication difficult. I had to contact the hotel staff through WhatsApp instead of using the in-room phone service. Another concern was the limited guest support regarding basic facilities. When I requested an iron for my clothes, security informed me that it could only be provided for 45 minutes, which was inconvenient for guests staying at the property. Overall, I found Room 124 to be uncomfortable and below the standard expected for hotel accommodation. Furthermore, the breakfast menu remained the same every day without variety, and I believe the hotel should improve both the quality of service and guest experience. Based on my personal experience, I would recommend travellers consider alternative accommodation options in Durban, such as the Royal Palm Hotel in Umhlanga, which may provide a more comfortable and professional stay. I sincerely hope Pavilion Hotel takes this feedback positively and works toward improving its customer service and room quality for future guests.

text: We truly enjoyed our stay at Pavilion Hotel and were deeply impressed by the level of service we received. From the moment we arrived, everything was warm, professional, and welcoming. The breakfast buffet was absolutely excellent fresh, well-prepared, and a perfect start to each day. A very special and sincere thank you goes to Pearl and Deshni for going above and beyond to make my wife’s birthday unforgettable. They surprised us by beautifully decorating our room at no extra cost, a gesture that touched our hearts and made the celebration incredibly special. This is what world-class service looks like thoughtful, genuine, and full of care. We will definitely return and highly recommend Pavilion Hotel to anyone looking for comfort, quality, and exceptional hospitality.

author: Riaz Ismail
text: I stayed here for two nights and unfortunately my experience was really disappointing. Before checking in, I specifically asked about the air conditioning and was assured everything was in order. When I got to my room, the aircon wasn’t working at all. I called for assistance and no one came. I called a second time and still nothing was done. I eventually had to go downstairs myself, and only then was I moved to another room, about 40 minutes after first reporting the issue. That already set the tone, but it didn’t end there. The next morning, I put the “Make Up My Room” sign on the door at 07:55am. When I returned at 23:00 that night, the room had not been cleaned or serviced at all. I informed reception, and I was told they would speak to the housekeeping manager, but the room still wasn’t cleaned and I received no follow-up. Although, someone did come knocking at my door at midnight to bring me towels. On top of that, guests were quite noisy in the hallways, which made the stay even less comfortable. Basic comfort, cleanliness, and a reasonable level of quiet are standard expectations at any hotel. Having to chase staff for assistance, deal with unresolved issues, and receive no follow-up is not acceptable. Really disappointing stay overall.

author: @ST-so-if
text: Un peu trop court à mon goût, un peu trop de parler pour si peu d’images, mais merci tout de même. J’y suis passé l’année dernière car mon fils est afro-descendant et nous avons fait la visite. Une journée merveilleuse en tous points, cette île est chargée d’une histoire lourde et tragique, mais tellement belle ! La maison des esclaves m’a énormément émue et marquée tant les murs et le lieu sont chargés de vibrations de souffrance, de tristesse et de douleurs intenses, j’en fus même honteuse d’être blanche et descendante de ces ignobles blancs, mais une femme sénégalaise avec qui j.ai échangé m’a dit que je ne devais pas culpabiliser, mais comment ne pas se sentir coupable de ce qu’ont fait nos ancêtres.... Au détour des ruelles tous ces artistes qui exposent leurs peintures, leurs créations avec des objets du quotidien recyclés en œuvres d’art, un régal pour les yeux. Et au delà de tout ça l’échange avec les gens qui vivent ou travaillent là, était vraiment positifs, si tant est qu’on cherche à communiquer bien sûr. Bref cette île est juste sublime et un petit détail qui m’a beaucoup plu, ce sont les pilonnes électriques camouflés en énormes palmiers, j’ai trouvé ça super !

text: La vidéo m’a fait sourire. C’est à 90% la même chose qu’en Côte d’Ivoire. Il est très facile pour les taxis de savoir que tu es un étranger. Il faut donc casser le prix en deux quand le chauffeur donne un tarif. Que tu sois un local ou pas, il faut négocier fort. Par contre, je partage complètement l’avis sur le fait de ne pas trop négocier les prix pour les articles dans les magasins artisanaux. Pour les adresses, il y a énormément d’enseignes qui sont enregistrées sur Google maps. Donc c’est bien pour se repérer pour être sûr que le taxi va bien a l’adresse indiquée et pour savoir quand dire stop. Vu qu’eux ils se repèrent avec de grandes enseignes, c’est au client de dire stop pour qu’ils s’arrêtent exactement là où vous désirez aller. En Côte d’Ivoire, on n’a pas de langue nationale forte comme le Wolof (on a plus de 60 langues mais il n’y en a pas une qui est parlé par tous. Cependant il y a 3 langues majoritaires qui sont le Dioula, Baoulé et Bété) . Tout le monde parle majoritairement le français mais très imprégné du nouchi qui est un mélange de plusieurs mots de nos différentes langues et du français. Merci pour la vidéo. Le Sénégal fait parti de la liste de mes pays à absolument voir. J’ai hâte d’y aller.

Ok si tu souhaites un hôtel vraiment luxueux tu payeras ce prix la mais si tu es en mode sac à dos et que ton but est de voyager pas trop cher, tu trouveras facilement des chambres à 15€ la nuit. Sur Airbnb il y a plethores d appartement et même de villa à 30 euros la nuit . La nourriture dans la rue c est 3 à 4€ maxi. Les taxis si tu connais les prix c est pas cher du tout, (sauf peut être à Dakar) mais le long des axes principaux tu trouveras des taxi clandos(collectif) le prix d une course est de 100 Franc CFA ( 15 centimes d euros) si tu restes dans la ville. Ils sont facilement reconnaissable, ce sont de très vieilles voitures cabossées avec 7-8 places a l intérieur. Lorsque l on connaît le pays et que l on parle aux gens on commence à connaître le prix réel et pourtant je ne parle pas Wolof et je suis toubab. Voilà je voulais apporter cette petite rectification. Pour info je suis actuellement à M'Bour, ville située sur la Petite côte

author: @chantelleglover-e3y
text: Comments here are so funny . Its nothing to do with aerodynamics or traction ( you dont see landspeed record vehicles with treaded grip on salt flats , its all bald tyres mainly ) . Sand is like no other medium, its not like tarmac or mud . When you hit above 60 mph on sand the front wheel will start to plow sand rather than run over it , as it ploughs the side tread grips from side to side and thats when the bars want to buck your hands off violently. The difference in riders is keeping constant contact with only the centre spine of the front wheel on the sand with less side tread touching . It literally is the skill to judge the difference of MM of contact on the front which stops the front end from wobbling .

author: @phpn99
text: I'm white. Been living in and out of Dakar for 30 years. As any city it has its down sides but overall it's been a wonderful place to live in. The people are very engaging ; the weather's great ; crime's low and you pretty much find everything you need, within limits. The major problem in Senegal is the demographic expansion — people are born faster than the economy can accommodate, so major urban centres are getting crowded and the job market is very bad. Nevertheless, the Senegalese keep a positive mindset and things rarely turn ugly. As a tourist spot, do not expect Paris or Orlando, and the beaches in Senegal aren't those of the Caribbean... but for open-minded adults willing to step out of their comfort zone, they'll discover a wonderful people and a rich culture that will broaden one's existential outlook.

author: @holdenackerman8783
text: A few quick tips with the airport: There is a shuttle bus that goes from the airport to downtown Dakar near the Palais de Justice. Cheap, easy, and comfy. If you go with a taxi, remember prices are negotiated in advance and drivers will try and price gouge. They will offer to take the expressway “Corniche” and ask for the toll from you, and then not take the exit. You can say you’ll pay the toll when you get there, but be ready to wait in traffic. Lastly, don’t exchange all your money at the airport - their rates are awful. It’s hard finding anyone who exchanges CFA outside Africa, but just get enough to get you into the city. Dakar is peppered with currency exchanges that offer much better rates. Glad you had fun Kyle! Never thought I’d see a City Profile Vid on Dakar. Goal is to go back next year - fingers crossed

text: I have traveled to Sénégal and Dakar for 2-week stays a handful of times to work with colleagues there. I am bilingual in French and English. It does help! I love many things about Sénégal and Dakar. The people and the hospitality are number one. The food is also wonderful. I love the beaches. My work brings me east of Dakar, nearer to Mbour, Kaolack, Fatick, and as remote as Gossas. I love the art, especially the painting, and have acquired several pieces over the years. Thank you for this portrait of Dakar and Sénégal. The Sénégalese are very enterprising, warm, and peaceful. I smile and laugh so much when I am there. Visit Sénégal if you want to experience authentic beaches and a warm culture.

text: As a Senegalese I would like to say thank you for showing my country, and most importantly showing both sides of life in Dakar, which is one of Africa's most expensive capital cities. I've been following your channel since that Haiti video in December 2022, showing the rough parts, things the traditional news channel won't show you. Big shoutout to Biggy, he has been an excellent guide. There's of course an explanation to why you have all these disparities in many hoods in Dakar. It has mostly to do with a lack of urban planning, some people build their houses in areas that are prone to flooding, while the government doesn't take enough actions to organize everything; add to that poverty, inflation, and social dynamics. Thus you have abandoned houses etc. The ghetto you visited is called Diamaguene located in Pikine while the nice neighbourhood is Fann Residence. We have one of the best weathers, only problem is the dust, due to the harmattan winds; expensive city but hopefully in 3 to 4 years it'll change. Cheers !!!

author: DW News
text: [Music] Modu Tun is returning to a place full of bad memories. 10 years ago, he paid €500 to take a fishing boat to the Canary Islands, the Spanish province off the west coast of Africa. Modu thought he would have a better life there and be able to send

author: DW News
text: money back to his family in Sagal. I started out on this very beach, but the trip was so risky. I'll never do anything like that again. Life and death are no longer in your hands. Those six days were the worst days of my life. Tune was picked up by the Spanish

author: DW News
text: Coast Guard and immediately deported back to Sagal. Since then, the tide of migrants has fallen to a trickle and the village has returned to fishing. The reason that those boats are not leaving for Europe anymore is mainly because of the increased border patrols

author: DW News
text: on the Spanish sites. People who still want to get to Europe choose other routes like the ones through Libya. But some people also say that the economic situation here has slowly improved. One of those optimists is the deputy mayor of Cayar. While he agrees that

author: DW News
text: fishing has its problems, that the hospital is often overcrowded and the schools could be better, he says the population is growing and that he says is proof of the upswing. In the high season for nine months of the year, people come from all over Sagal to work in the fishing

author: DW News
text: industry. The fishermen here have made big efforts to improve their situation and to protect the resources. Even agriculture has developed considerably. People are attracted here from all around the region. But for farmer Alio, it's not been easy. He used to

author: DW News
text: irrigate his fields with a diesel pump, which turned out to be too expensive. His field dried out and he couldn't compete with cheap vegetables imported from Europe. Now with development aid from Germany, he uses a solar pump, a more sustainable solution. He's optimistic

author: DW News
text: that his seven children will also have a future as farmers. If young people see a future for themselves here, they'll stop wanting to leave. They'll want the same life as everybody else here. My neighbors ask me how they can get a system like mine because they can see how well it

author: DW News
text: works for me. Modu Tune is now chairman of an organization for migrants who've returned. They have more than 500 members. After Tune's bad experiences, he's well qualified to tell young people about the dangers of illegal migration. When I give young people advice, I say

author: DW News
text: don't do it. But if they're determined, I tell them they should try to find a legal way with a visa and a passport, but not those deadly boats. Thousands of young Africans have drowned going that way. Tune has set a good example. He has a job in a fish factory, three children,

author: DW News
text: and his own car. He says it's now entirely possible to find success at home in Sagal.

text: I just landed back in the states after two weeks in Cairo where I rented a car. While it is DAUNTING on first view, it’s actually very easy to navigate once you overcome the initial hecticness of it all. There’s a very good ebb and flow about it all which after 2 weeks behind the wheel, I didn’t encounter any accidents. Not one. There are unwritten rules of the road that everyone knows and follows. Don’t cut people off and become defensive. Rather, understand that you go, than I go. I allow you in, you allow me in later and Vice versa. Once that basic fundamental is obtained, the rest is easy as anywhere else. The laws are just suggestions but follow the code of the streets and you’ll do just fine. Overreacting to anything and everything may just well give you a panic attack lol

author: @karimanshahine3224
text: I'm not sure how long this is gonna be but it's worth reading in case you concider visiting Egypt. Okay so I'm egyptian and I have some re- correction on the video as an Egyptian citizen here just to clear things up a little more and hopefully help some people who consider visuting egypt,So for tip no.(1): Yes, you should avoid PDA as that kind of contact isn not traditionally allowed, but any other friendly gestures as of hugging and a peck on the cheek or wherever is fine. Tip no. (2): Actually that's a very requested advice I would give to anyone considering visiting egypt as egypt is full of amazing places to vist, it's not just all about the sand and the pyramids and the Pharoahs trust me there is so much more than you can think of so you should definitely hire a tour guide for a better experience. Tip no.(3): Let's get this straight, now if you are visiting a coastal area you can pretty much wear anything (men&women), if you are visiting the suburbs of egypt you should prevent showing skin as much as you can, because as said the locals here prefer modest dressing or as much as you can possibility get to that, and if you are visiting any other places apart from the above then you should just stick in between, in other words for men you can pretty much wear whatever you want, and for women you should just prevent showing skin as much as you can possibly can, you can wear jeans, t-shirts, dresses, blouses, a lot of choices not including hijab as you don't HAVE to wear that. Tip no. (4): local shops here are considered the cheapest way to buy pretty much everything as they are the go to for anyone who can't afford the amount of money it might cost anywhere else, so for tourists those shops (or those individuals) are quite cheap so most of them double the price for tourists, so expect that if you consider buying anything from local sellers ONLY. Tip no. (5): This one is a bit unnecessary as you should always be careful when you are crossing the street pretty much anywhere, however, if you ever had a difficulty while doing so you can always ask someone to help you or someone will approach you without you asking as most people are very nice and friendly here especially with non-citizens, and also most of them would love to help and approach you even asking for pictures without expecting anything for return, so yeah expect that as well. Tip no. (6): Unless you KNOW what you are signing up for don't take any part in it. Also, why would you hire someone in the street anyway ? trust me tour gides in egypt are not as expensive as you might think. Tip no. (7): You don't HAVE to tip anyone. You can but you don't have to do it. a lot of people expect you to tip them but you are not forced to. Tip no. (8): Yes, a lot of areas here have street animals but not most of them are dangerous just prevent to get as near them for caution only. Tip no. (9): Try your best to follow this tip as it's taken more seriously here, it's not common to stumble into someone who is drunk and yes it's considered a crime in some areas, so be careful. Tip no. (10): I mean, some people don't really care about timing, and some others take timing very seriously, it's not a community thing, but a matter of fact it's usually very crowdy here so be careful with that if you want to get to a place on time. I hope that was helpful enough & please if you have any questions hit me up in the comment section and I will gladly tell you whatever you need to know! have a great day :))♥

author: @DIALOGO2012
text: IMPOSSÍVEL! O EGITO ESTAVA NA IDADE DO BRONZE Olha, a teoria dos construtores egípicios tem sido contestada por muitos especialistas! Porque hoje com toda a tecnologia de construção, com corte de blocos de pedra com gigantescas serra elétrica, corte com laser, guindastes, carretas, etc.. seria uma obra de proporções fora do comum para a engenharia atual. No tempo em que as pirâmides foram construídas (4500AC) a região ainda estava na idade do bronze, ou seja só havia ferramentas do cobre e marretas de Madeira. A grande pirâmide foi construída com 2 milhões e 300 mil blocos de pedra calcária extraídas, cortados e polidos. Há estimativa que a grande pirâmide de Quéops foi construída em 20 anos, é que dentro dessa prazo os operários egípicios teriam que colocar 316 blocos de pedra pesando entre 2 a 15 toneladas na grande pirâmide, trazidos da pedreira de Assuã fica a uma distância da grande pirâmide de 800kM, sem contar os blocos de mármore e diorita pedras extremamente duras no interior da grande pirâmide com peso de até 80 toneladas, tendo formas impossíveis de se conseguir na época! Outro questionamento é como os construtores egípicios conseguiram colocar blocos de 2 a 15 toneladas nas partes superiores da pirâmide Quéops, porque na época não existia guindaste como os de hoje (lembro que existe o argumento a favor dos egípicios de construíram uma rampa para colocar os blocos conforme a pirâmide ida subindo. Porém, também essa teoria é rejeitada, seria um volume de blocos de pedra calcária igual ou superior ao da grande pirâmide para construir a rampa, sendo o trabalho e o tempo o dobro para fazer toda a obra). Outro ponto questionado são os cortes realizados nos blocos de pedra no interior da pirâmide, os blocos do interior da pirâmide é um tipo muito mais duro como o mármore ou diorita, que apresentam cortes para adquirirem formas impossível para a época, são cortes retos, curvos, se tais cortes fossem feitos com laser não teriam a mesma perfeição (e tudo isso para uma civilização que ainda estava na idade do bronze!). Realmente essa obra contrária a lógica da razão e a matemática da engenharia, por isso tudo não dá para acreditar que os egípicios de 4500 AC construíram tantas obras de proporções megalíticas com detalhes de engenharia MODERNA! Faz um teste: pega uma talhadeira de cobre e retire um bloco de 15 toneladas de pedra calcária na pedreira, se conseguir extrair, corte o bloco na forma de cubo e depois faça o polimento (precisa ser polido para encaixar de forma perfeita um no outro), conseguiu? Agora com a mesma talhadeira de cobre retire um bloco de mármore ou um bloco de DIURITA e corte no formato cubo e depois faça o polimento, são 316 por dia! Você vai perceber que essa tarefa excede a capacidade de 100mil operários!

text: They tell you the Egyptians built the pyramids. But the Egyptians themselves never said that. They spoke of Zep Tepi — “The First Time.” A primordial era before pharaohs, before dynasties, before recorded history. An age when the “First Ones” walked the Earth and established cosmic order. And what did they say about the greatest structures? They already stood. They did not claim to have built them. They said they inherited them. Look at the evidence: Worker graffiti appears only in hidden relieving chambers — proof of later work, not original construction. Carbon dating covers only mortar and organic debris — never the stone itself. The largest pyramids contain no original bodies or burial goods. No contemporary inscription from the Fourth Dynasty says “We built this.” After the Great Pyramid, nothing of comparable scale or precision was ever built again. They were there. They worked there. They expanded and used the site. They even claimed ideological ownership. But they never once said they raised these monuments from bare bedrock. Instead, across Pyramid Texts, Coffin Texts, and the Book of the Dead, they consistently pointed backward: “Houses which stand since the First Time” (PT 316) “Walls not raised by any man” (PT 524) “Foundations laid in the First Time” (PT 478–482) “A place made before humankind” (PT 697) So the question is not wild speculation. It is simple and direct: If the Egyptians themselves never claimed to have built the greatest pyramids from scratch — why do we insist that they did? Perhaps we should stop projecting our assumptions onto them and start listening to what they actually said. ∇ EN-99 Δ

author: @MY_99Kapsula
text: They tell you the Egyptians built the pyramids. But the Egyptians themselves never said that. They spoke of Zep Tepi — “The First Time.” A primordial era before pharaohs, before dynasties, before recorded history. An age when the “First Ones” walked the Earth and established cosmic order. And what did they say about the greatest structures? They already stood. They did not claim to have built them. They said they inherited them. Look at the evidence: Worker graffiti appears only in hidden relieving chambers — proof of later work, not original construction. Carbon dating covers only mortar and organic debris — never the stone itself. The largest pyramids contain no original bodies or burial goods. No contemporary inscription from the Fourth Dynasty says “We built this.” After the Great Pyramid, nothing of comparable scale or precision was ever built again. They were there. They worked there. They expanded and used the site. They even claimed ideological ownership. But they never once said they raised these monuments from bare bedrock. Instead, across Pyramid Texts, Coffin Texts, and the Book of the Dead, they consistently pointed backward: “Houses which stand since the First Time” (PT 316) “Walls not raised by any man” (PT 524) “Foundations laid in the First Time” (PT 478–482) “A place made before humankind” (PT 697) So the question is not wild speculation. It is simple and direct: If the Egyptians themselves never claimed to have built the greatest pyramids from scratch — why do we insist that they did? Perhaps we should stop projecting our assumptions onto them and start listening to what they actually said. Pyramid Texts (PT), Coffin Texts (CT), and Book of the Dead (BD), with exact verse numbers and citations. 🔹 Corpus Number / Verse Quote (translation of the meaning) Interpretation PT 316 "Houses which stand since the First Time" / "The king enters the houses which stand since Zep Tepi" inherited PT 600 "The road built in the First Time by the gods" inherited PT 254 "What was done in the First Time" inherited PT 1466–1468 "The heritage of the First Time belongs to me" PT 1100 "The steps built by the gods" inherited PT 2081–2082 “The stone house the gods established” inherited PT 478–482 “Foundations laid in the First Time” inherited PT 364–366 "The road of the First Time" inherited PT 524 "Walls not raised by any man" inherited PT 697 "A place made before humankind" inherited CT 1130 "In the time of the First Ones, when light was the only king" inherited/pre-human era CT 335 "Those who became Akh in the First Time" inherited/pre-human era CT 74–78 "Before human names appeared, gates were opened without words" inherited / pre-human era BD 17 "I am the light which was before the light; I am the lord of those who were before the gods" inherited / pre-human era BD 80 "I am one of the predecessors who directed the roads of heaven" inherited / pre-human era BD 110 "Those who departed in the First Time, to the land of northern light" inherited / pre-human era BD 175 "The Rule of the First Ones Whose Names Are Not Known" Inherited / Pre-Human Era 🔹 Number of Places in Egyptian Texts Referring to Inheritance / "First Ones": 17 Number of Places Claiming that the Pharaohs Built the Pyramids from Scratch: 0 This clearly demonstrates that even the oldest sources convey memories of a pre-dynastic civilization or structures that the Pharaohs later merely inherited and, to some extent, adapted for their ritual purposes. One could, of course, say, "it's just symbolism." But then we must explain why this symbolism looks completely different in ordinary temples than in pyramids. Nowhere in Egyptian texts do we find a sentence like: "We, the Egyptians of the 4th Dynasty, built these pyramids from the foundations." "Cheops commissioned the construction of the Great Pyramid in the year X." Instead, they consistently use the language of heritage and the First Time (Zep Tepi). This is not a linguistic accident. It is a choice. When the Egyptians wanted to say that they built something, they were able to do so very clearly. They did this with temples, obelisks, statues, canals – wherever they were actually the builders. At the largest pyramids in Giza, they suddenly change the language to: "houses standing from the First Time" "walls that no man built" "foundations laid before humanity" This is not a description of "operational reality." This is a description of the origins of these structures – and they clearly indicate that they were not their creators. Conclusion: The Egyptians described symbolic, ritual, and cosmic reality with incredible precision. However, when it comes to the material origins of the largest pyramids – they consistently referred to something older than themselves. Ignoring this distinction is disrespectful to the texts. It is a selective reading. 𓆑 𓂀 𓇳 𓆣 The Inventory Stela is a significant archaeological artifact that raises important questions about the history of monumental architecture in ancient Egypt. Content: Mentions Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops) but describes him as a restorer rather than the original builder of the structures, including the Temple of Isis, referred to as the “Mistress of the Pyramid.” Debunking "Key Facts" These two elements (the name Akhet-Khufu and the "Friends of Khufu" graffiti) are most often cited as "irrefutable evidence," so it's worth taking a closer look. 1. Akhet-Khufu – "Khufu's Horizon" Yes, the Great Pyramid was officially called Akhet-Khufu. However, this name doesn't automatically mean "Khufu built it." Pharaohs often gave their names to existing sacred sites, temples, or monuments to claim them ideologically. This was an act of legitimization, not necessarily a declaration of "I built this from scratch." 2. "Friends of Khufu" graffiti in the relief chambers These symbols do exist and are important evidence. However, their interpretation is often simplified. What exactly do they prove? That construction/assembly work was underway there during Khufu's time (specifically, the heavy granite ceiling beams were being placed above the King's Chamber). That there was an organized crew of workers who used this name. What do they NOT prove? That Khufu was the creator of the entire pyramid from foundation to summit. That the pyramid did not have an older core or an earlier construction phase. It's like finding the signature of a renovation crew in the attic of an old castle and claiming, on this basis, that this crew built the entire castle from the foundations. Both elements (the name Akhet-Khufu and the graffiti) are evidence of Khufu's activity on the Giza Plateau. The question, however, is: Does activity equal full authorship from scratch? The Egyptians themselves consistently used the language of inheritance and the "First Time" in their oldest religious texts, not the language of "we built from the foundations." Egyptians of the Fourth Dynasty worked on the Giza Plateau, expanding and utilizing these monuments, and then ideologically claimed them for themselves. But whether they built them entirely from scratch – we don't know for sure. And the Egyptians themselves never explicitly stated this. This is not "alternative history." This is simply an acknowledgment of the limits of our current knowledge. 𓆑 𓂀 𓇳 𓆣 Global Context Sumer: “The king restored an ancient temple that had always been there.” Incas: “Works of the First Men,” “Stone that was already here.” Nan Madol: “Created by people who could fly.” India: “Cities from previous cycles, found after cataclysms.” Anatolia: “We will excavate, we will not build.” Megalithic Europe: “Foundations of the giants.” Conclusion: The narrative pattern “we inherited, we did not build” appears independently on all continents → indicates the historical legacy of a global engineering tradition. ∇ EN-99 Δ 𓆑 𓂀 𓇳 𓆣

author: @OnlyScienceRules
text: 1. Who Built Them? Skilled Egyptian Labourers — Not Slaves Archaeological findings from Giza (workers’ villages, bakeries, medical facilities, payroll-like systems, grave goods) show that the workforce consisted of: • Permanent skilled workers (stone masons, engineers, architects, surveyors) • Rotating seasonal labourers (farmers during the Nile flood season) These were paid, respected workers, not slaves. ⸻ 2. Quarrying the Stone Limestone (main blocks) Most limestone was quarried directly at Giza, adjacent to the pyramids. Granite (internal chambers, structural supports) Granite came from Aswan, 800 km south, transported by barges along the Nile. Tools: • Copper chisels • Dolerite pounding stones • Wooden sledges • Ropes (probably plant-based, very strong) No iron tools at that period. ⸻ 3. Moving the Blocks The Sledge-on-Sand System The dominant supported method: Workers pulled stone blocks on wooden sledges. A painting from Djehutihotep’s tomb shows a man pouring water on sand. Modern physics experiments show: • Wetting sand reduces friction by ~50% • The shear strength of damp sand allows heavy loads to slide effectively This single detail explains a huge part of the logistics. Numbers Estimates for Cheops (Great Pyramid): • Blocks: ~2.3 million • Average weight: 2.5 tonnes • Workforce: ~10–20k at any one time (not 100k+) ⸻ 4. How Did They Raise the Stones? This is the most debated part, but the consensus is a combination of: ⸻ (A) A Long External Ramp (for lower levels) Wide, straight, gently sloping ramp made from: • Limestone chips • Clay • Shale • Rubble Used for the first ~30–40% of the pyramid’s height. Evidence: • Remains of large ramps found at several pyramid sites (not Giza’s — likely removed after construction) ⸻ (B) Spiral or Zig-Zag Ramps (higher levels) Likely used as the pyramid grew in height and a huge single ramp became impractical. Possibilities supported by the evidence: • A spiral ramp hugging the outside • L-shaped ramps built against temporary terraces • Internal ramps with access shafts (Jean-Pierre Houdin’s theory — plausible, though still debated) ⸻ (C) Counterweight Systems for Very Heavy Blocks Internal chambers and ceiling blocks weighing 20–70 tonnes likely used: • Counterweight sledges • Gravity-assisted lifting • Simple cranes (wooden, lever-based) inside chamber spaces No evidence of advanced machinery, just clever engineering. ⸻ 5. Leveling + Precision One of the most impressive aspects is the precision: • Base is level within 2 cm • Cardinal alignment is nearly perfect Methods: • Water-filled trenches for leveling • Gnomons (vertical sticks) and shadow measurements • Simple ropes and plumb bobs for right angles • Astronomical alignment using circumpolar stars ⸻ 6. Organising the Workforce Evidence from worker villages shows: • Work gangs of 40–100 men • Teams named humorously (“Friends of Khufu,” etc.) • Supply chains for food, water, tools, and medical care • Rotational 3-month labour shifts during Nile flooding Mortuary archaeology shows healed bones, medical treatment, and good diets, indicating well-cared-for workers. ⸻ 7. Timeline Building the Great Pyramid took: • ~20–27 years This is entirely feasible with: • Labour: 10–20k • Rate: ~300 blocks/day • Stone source: on-site • Seasonal labour surges ⸻ 8. Debunking Popular Myths ❌ Aliens No evidence. Everything aligns with known technology. ❌ Impossible precision Actually within the capabilities of hand tools + geometry. ❌ Too heavy to move Experiments show a team of 20 can move a 2.5-tonne block on a sledge with wetted sand. ❌ Slaves Completely disproven by archaeology. ⸻ In Summary The pyramids were built by: • Skilled Egyptian workers • Using stone quarries on-site, wooden sledges, water lubrication, long and spiral ramps, counterweights, geometry, and sophisticated organisation. • Across 20–30 years with a surprisingly small but well-managed labour force. Nothing supernatural — just human ingenuity, engineering, planning, and social organisation at an extraordinary scale. Thank you technology, thank you science & collective academic knowledge, thank you ChatGPT.

text: It's my country! Egypt is a country with a rich cultural and historical heritage, and there are many places to visit in the country beyond just the pyramids. Some of the top destinations include Cairo, the capital city with its vibrant atmosphere and famous landmarks like the Citadel, al-Hazar Park, and the Cairo Tower. Giza is home to the famous pyramids and the Great Sphinx of Giza. Alexandria is a port city known for its historic Library and modern amenities, while Luxor is famous for its temples and necropolises. Aswan is a city to learn about the Nubian culture and visit its temples, museums, and beaches. The Red Sea is a popular destination for diving and offers clear waters and diverse marine life. Fayum is an oasis known for its abundance of wildlife and history, while Marsa Matruh and Hurghada are popular resorts for their beaches and diving opportunities. Charm el Sheikh is another resort town known for its beaches and coral reefs.

text: We're actually in Sharm right now. This is our second year here. My husband and I were laughing at the "do not enter a shop, or the door will be closed and the family will come down." This happened to us last year- we entered a shop after being asked to go in, and he closed the door behind us. It was a bit scary, but he made us tea and showed us just about everything for sale in his shop. In the end, to make a getaway, we bought some (horrendously overpriced) camel milk moisturiser and a massive bag of loose tea leaves. The forceful approach is a bit much, but we learned our lesson and won't be entering this year 😂.

author: @sarahwalton2662
text: I've been to Sharm multiple times and just love it. I want to add a comment about the amazing friendliness and hospitality of the Egyptian people you will meet. Yes it will be predominately men, however as a solo female traveller they are always nothing but kind and respectful. Also, seeing how they interact with parents, and especially the children is fantastic. If you have young children don't be concerned by this familiarity - which can include picking the kids up and showing them a lot of positive attention. It's just the way people are in Egypt, and the Middle East in general..... kind, caring, respectful, and so very generous. Btw the vendors will harrass you, but this has been their way of working for more than a hundred years (read Agatha Christie's Death on the Nile which also mentions it and was published in 1937). For me - the #1 draw is the underwater world... however Sharm has so much to offer as your video shows.

author: @pgr3290
text: In Egypt or Turkey or many places outside the EU the best bet is to simply buy a local SIM card or a tourist SIM, which is preloaded with loads of data and is usually not very expensive. You can get them at arrivals in the airport or in some shops. Turkcell is best in Turkey, Vodafone usually best coverage in Egypt. I think in Egypt it is something like £7 for 10GB or £15 for 30GB which you'll probably never use even over a couple weeks of holiday. Reason why this is so great in Egypt is because Uber exists! In Hurghada, Cairo, Alexandria and a few other spots you can hit up an Uber- no haggling, no arguing or tips- just cheap taxis. Sharm has yet to have Uber so that's a shame but wait and see.

text: Is Homework Good or Not? A Balanced Perspective Homework has been a cornerstone of education systems around the world for generations. While some view it as an essential tool for reinforcing classroom learning, others argue it causes unnecessary stress and encroaches on students’ personal time. The debate over the value of homework continues to gain momentum, especially as new educational philosophies and teaching methods evolve. So, is homework good or not? The answer isn’t black and white—it depends on various factors, including the quality, quantity, and purpose of the homework assigned. This essay will explore the pros and cons of homework, examine research findings, and offer a balanced conclusion. Benefits of Homework One of the primary arguments in favor of homework is that it reinforces what students learn in class. Just like practicing a sport or musical instrument, repeated exposure to academic concepts helps students internalize and master them. Homework allows students to review lessons at their own pace, solidifying their understanding outside the often fast-paced classroom environment. Another advantage of homework is that it fosters important life skills such as time management, responsibility, and self-discipline. When students are tasked with assignments to complete on their own, they learn to plan, prioritize, and meet deadlines—skills that are crucial in both academic and professional life. Homework can also provide parents with insight into what their children are learning, encouraging family involvement and support in the educational process. Moreover, homework can help teachers assess student understanding. By reviewing completed assignments, teachers can identify areas where students are struggling and adjust their teaching strategies accordingly. This feedback loop can lead to more effective instruction and better outcomes for students. Drawbacks of Homework Despite its benefits, homework also has its drawbacks. Critics argue that too much homework can lead to stress, burnout, and a negative attitude toward learning. In younger students especially, large amounts of homework can diminish the time available for rest, play, and family interaction—activities that are equally important for healthy development. Another concern is that not all homework is meaningful or effective. Sometimes, students are given busywork that doesn’t contribute to real learning. When homework assignments are repetitive or disconnected from the curriculum, they can feel like a burden rather than a learning tool. Equity is also an important issue. Not all students have the same resources or support systems at home. Those from disadvantaged backgrounds may lack access to a quiet workspace, internet connection, or parental help. As a result, homework can widen the achievement gap between students from different socio-economic backgrounds. Furthermore, excessive homework can lead to academic dishonesty. When students are overwhelmed or don’t understand the material, they may be tempted to copy answers from classmates or the internet, undermining the learning process. Research Findings Research on the effectiveness of homework provides mixed results. According to studies by education researcher Harris Cooper, moderate amounts of homework can be beneficial, especially for high school students. Cooper found that for older students, homework is positively correlated with academic achievement, but the same is not true for elementary school students, where the benefits are minimal or nonexistent. The National PTA and the National Education Association recommend the “10-minute rule,” which suggests 10 minutes of homework per grade level per night. For example, a third grader should have about 30 minutes of homework each night, while a high school senior might have up to two hours. This guideline aims to strike a balance between reinforcing learning and avoiding overload. In countries like Finland, known for their top-performing education systems, students have relatively little homework. Finnish educators prioritize high-quality instruction during school hours and emphasize the importance of play and family time after school. This model has prompted educators worldwide to reconsider the role of homework in academic success. Homework in the Digital Age The digital age has transformed the way homework is assigned and completed. Online learning platforms, educational apps, and digital collaboration tools have made homework more interactive and accessible. At the same time, screen fatigue and distractions from technology can pose challenges for students trying to focus on assignments. Technology also raises concerns about academic integrity. With answers readily available online, students may be tempted to take shortcuts instead of developing their critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Teachers must be mindful of these issues and design assignments that encourage original thought and engagement. Balancing Homework Effectively Given the mixed evidence and varied experiences, the key to making homework effective lies in balance. Educators should ensure that homework is purposeful, relevant, and aligned with learning objectives. It should challenge students without overwhelming them, and it should provide opportunities for practice, application, and reflection. Parents and guardians also play a crucial role in supporting their children’s homework habits. Creating a structured routine, offering encouragement, and communicating with teachers can help students stay motivated and manage their workload effectively. Policymakers and school administrators should consider flexible homework policies that take into account students’ diverse needs and circumstances. Rather than enforcing blanket homework requirements, schools can adopt individualized approaches that support student well-being and academic growth. Conclusion So, is homework good or not? The answer depends on how it is used. When thoughtfully designed and appropriately assigned, homework can be a valuable tool for reinforcing learning, developing responsibility, and enhancing academic performance—particularly for older students. However, when overused or poorly implemented, homework can cause stress, hinder personal development, and exacerbate inequalities. Ultimately, the goal should not be to eliminate homework entirely, but to improve its quality and purpose. Education is most effective when it supports the whole child—academically, emotionally, and socially. By striking a thoughtful balance, educators and families can ensure that homework contributes positively to a student’s overall educational experience.

author: @omowaleds963
text: I grew up in the southern part of the United States. Almost everything you said my dear departed grandmother would agree with. I have heard very old people talk of ghost or spirits walking backwards. Even today women will spread the palms of their hands at a person during an argument or to show disdain, hostility or irritation. And even you my sister remind me of my family members with your gestures and your style. One morning I was at my grandmothers house in the kitchen when I noticed a spider on the kitchen door. I immediately took off my shoe to kill the spider. But my grandmother stopped me. Her words were firm, forceful but still spoken with love:"Don't kill it...let go outside...don't kill it..." I carefully guided the spider away from the door and it quickly crawled away. I was surprised and confused. I asked her why she didn't want me to kill the spider. She looked down a me and stared at me. I could tell she was going to tell me something very deep and very serious. "The old folks use to say that sometimes our ancestors come to visit us in different forms......that's what the old folks use to say...." My grandmother was born in 1888. She was a deity to me and what she said was true and I believed it! Of course I was still confused but I remained silent. Only years later did I really understand her beautiful Africaness. Sometimes I would go with my grandmother when she went shopping. I would carry the bags for her and sometimes I would carry live chickens to her home . During a summer thunder storm, all the children would have to come into the house and be absolutely quiet. All the radios, televisions, lights, everything was turned off. When the lightening flashed and the thunder rolled it was God was doing his work. No talking. No playing. No moving around. During those days people made a pallet on the floor and the children would more than likely go to sleep. The adults would talk quietly until the storm was over. Even today many people I know will not talk on the telephone during a thunder storm. Thank you

Hey, I know O! *Please remind subscribers to click on the bell, or the won't receive notifications when your new videos come out.* I was wondering if you might investigate something for us in the future regarding domestic air travel in the South West. text: Thanks Sassy Funke, you're always on point! Just a quick tip... For those in the US who do not have the money to pay for their tickets in full, I recently just heard about a website (https://www.airfordable.com/) that allows you put your flight ticket on a layaway plan. You make a down payment and then make monthly or bi-weekly payments to pay up the balance of the ticket. I used the site when I was travelling to Lagos last December and I wasn't disappointed at all. It helped me plan way ahead (even though I didn't have the full payment at the time that I bought it), and it also helped me save for the trip too. The only downside is that there may be a service charge which you can still be able to reduce if you find someone that already has an account with them. All in all, it is a very good way to go about travelling in December.

text: Hi Flo Chinyere thanks for your videos. My lovely wife’s name is Chinyere & I am not surprised that people who answer Chinyere do good things 😁. Just a little comment about the origin of the name “Okada” for the Nigerian commercial motorcyclists. Yes, there is a village close to Benin called Okada. Then Chief Igbinedion from Benin City owned an airline in the 80s called Okada airlines. In 1987/88 Chief Igbinedion donated about 1 million Naira (a very huge sum of money then) to the commercial motorcyclists’ association in Benin City then. They were overjoyed. The cyclists took to the streets and started to announce that their new name was “Okada” after Okada airlines. The name has stuck with all commercial motorcyclists in Nigeria since then even after the Okada airlines has gone out of business.

author: @gbemisolaolujobi5432
text: As a Yoruba-speaking Nigerian, I would like to quickly address the little communication gap that led to the Gary phenomenon, since it seems to be taking on a life of it's own. The catfish seller in the market didn't forget Nick's name and call him Gary. No! She said, "Let me take your picture, jare." Jare, ( which sounded like Gary) in Yoruba, the language of Southwest Nigeria, where Lagos is located, means 'Please' or 'If you please.' So she simply said, "Let me take your picture, please." Nigerians have a habit of injecting words from their local languages or dialects into their sentences when they speak English in informal situations. In the same way, when they speak their local languages, they inject English words into their sentences. So that's what happened. She said, "Let me take your picture, jare." ("Let me take your picture, please"). She didn't call him Gary! So, don't worry Nick. Your 'girlfriend' didn't forget your name!

text: I was born in Maiduguri. I stayed there with my family till I was 11 years old. It's a lovely city with nice people. I had a very good primary and secondary school foundation there. Business Model and Strategies: Capacity Filling: Ships often operate at over 100% capacity, filling third or fourth berths in cabins to maximize potential, even if base fares are low. Pre-booking Encouragement: Lines push to sell packages (drinks, dining, excursions) before the cruise begins to secure revenue early. Lower Tax Environments: Many cruise lines register in nations with lower corporate taxes, enhancing net profits. On average, for every passenger, roughly 70% of revenue comes from the fare, while nearly 30% is generated from onboard spending. Flags of Convenience (Open Registry): Countries like the Bahamas and Panama offer lenient regulations and lower taxes, allowing cruise lines to operate more cheaply than if registered in countries like the U.S.. Labor Supply: Developing nations, including the Philippines, Indonesia, and India, provide a significant portion of the workforce, offering competitive wages that are attractive to operators. Port of Call/Tourism Infrastructure: Countries invest in specialized port infrastructure to host ships, generating income through tourist spending on excursions, dining, and, for example, a 660 Euro average per passenger. Shipbuilding and Technical Services: Countries with advanced maritime engineering (e.g., Italy, France, Germany) secure contracts to build and maintain these massive vessels. Domestic/Niche Cruising: Some nations, such as the U.S., maintain a smaller, strictly regulated, domestically flagged fleet for specific routes (e.g., in Alaska or Hawaii) that comply with local labor laws. Infrastructure Development: Upgrading port facilities to handle passenger ships is essential. This includes developing dedicated, modern cruise terminals with easy access to attractions. Strategic Partnerships: Collaborating with stakeholders to create, market, and promote tailored cruise itineraries. Highlight Unique Offerings: Showcasing cultural heritage, eco-tourism, and wildlife to create distinct, high-value shore experiences. Streamlined Logistics: Simplifying visa processes and improving safety measures to make the destination attractive to travelers. Regional Cooperation: Working with neighboring countries to develop multi-destination routes that increase the appeal for longer, regional tours. Examples in Africa: Nigeria & Ivory Coast: These countries are investing in port infrastructure to accommodate more cruise ships. Kenya: Opened a new cruise terminal in Mombasa to boost tourism. South Africa: Utilizes a dedicated cruise terminal in Cape Town, which has successfully attracted multiple international cruise lines for seasonal homeporting.

Obudu Mountain Resort, formerly known as Obudu Cattle Ranch, is a breathtaking tourist destination located on the Obudu Plateau in Cross River State, Nigeria. Sitting at an elevation of 1,575 meters (5,200 feet) above sea level, it is famous for its cool, temperate climate and stunning rolling green hills. The Obudu Canopy Walkway: A thrilling 60-meter-long suspended swinging bridge that takes you high above the forest floor.The Holy Mountain: A popular peak known for its panoramic, sweeping views of the surrounding plateau and deep valleys.Waterfalls & Natural Pools: Several natural springs and cataracts dot the landscape, including the famous cascading Grotto.Horseback Riding: A relaxing way to explore the expansive, cloud-level pastures.Bonfires & Barbecues: Because mountain temperatures frequently drop below \(10^{\circ}C\) (\(50^{\circ}F\)), evenings often feature cozy bonfires and outdoor dining. Location: The resort is situated in Obanliku Local Government Area, close to the Cameroon border.Travel Logistics: Getting there is a journey. Visitors typically fly into Calabar or Enugu and then drive several hours to the base of the mountain. From there, you can drive up the winding, scenic mountain pass or take an aerial cable car.Accommodation: The resort offers a range of options, from standard hotel rooms and African-style huts to multi-bedroom villas. It is highly recommended to book in advance and confirm your room availability.
