text: Own a LR4 and have set it up for overland touring in Aus(180L fuel tank(1500km on road), Rear Wheel Carriers, Bullbar, full roof rack, switch for off-road height above 55km/h, etc etc etc) and I do agree with your comments to some extent Andrew. You do need to put in a little extra effort and dollars to set one up for remoteness as you need to purchase the small BT IID Tool which is a LR specific computer which can override all sensors on the car, It can be done, but not as easily as a low tech model. Parts are actually cheap i've found as long as you're willing to express ship direct from the UK. Really love mine and for me the air suspension is worth the trade off, it's that good.. Remembering though there are very few true 4x4's as described that don't require the wheel speed sensors to be functioning to keep driving down rough terrain... LC200 being an example. Some things on the LR4 are very easy to fix. I've replaced all 4 of my air struts last week with 200k kms on them in 3 hours with 2 jacks stands and a jack for example.

author: @AlternativPerspectiv
text: This is a very well-balanced report on Zimbabwe. I am genuinely surprised! Some things you may not be entirely clued up on. There are spies for the ruling party EVERYWHERE. That "Everyone is a policeman" statement by those two men was not necessarily true, but it is very close to the reality. If you cannot speak freely against the ruling party; you just don't know who is waiting to snap handcuffs on you for it. Those two might could very well have been spies monitoring you! The disused bridge/crosswalk is a symptom of Zimbabwe's problems. The ruling party acts with no interest at all for the people, but personal agrandizement, then legislates to protect itself from the people's wrath. The wealth you see flowing through then ice areas is mostly illicit whether directly or indirect; tenders that are dished out without any procurement process, to friends and family, mining licences, business licenses etc.. all restricted to 'outsides' but easily available to the connected. If you are succeeding in Zimbabwe either you are part of the connected elite... or you should have a Plan B because the elite will come for your business... and they will have the might of the government behind them. The same corruption and maladministration and political abuse is why you see a decrepit Harare. The ruling party, to diminish opposition support, legislated that all municipal revenue will be collected by the same municipality, then be directed to the state, then the state will dish out the same revenue BACK to the state. Clearly inefficient, but in so doing, the ruling party could authorize tender contracts for its friends who are then not held accountable. Look for Chin'ono's coverage on this issue. There is a company contract to clean up the city. It just doesn't bother. What are people to do? Protest? How? Where? When? To whom? So at the end of the day Zimbabweans are like the victim of domestic violence; when visitors come the abuser goes into "Best behaviour" mode and the visitors cannot imagine any abuse happening. The victim, on the other hand, is forced to smile and wave with heavy make up on to hide the bruises. That is Zimbabwe today. Good video!

text: I’ve been to see this tree twice. The first time was in 1993 and 1996. Up close it is magnificent and enormous, you incredibly small standing beside it. It is located in a protected forest reserve just outside Asamankese in the Akym (Akim) area, in the Eastern region. What struck us was the atmosphere in the forest around the tree. It was tangible! We could feel the spirit and power radiating out from the tree. We all immediately felt a profound sense of respect and humbleness being in its presence. We were shown a baby tree of the same species growing near by but these were the only two in the whole forest at the time. The guide told us that the tree was between 800-1000 years old so I hope it will keep growing. 🙏🏾

text: That Prekese as it is called by Ghanaians the lady gave you at the shop is also called Aidan fruit in English, Aridan or Oshosho by Nigerians. This is the fruit of Tetrapleura tetraptera. Its very healthy. You can make bitters from it either with alcohol or water by putting the pieces of the fruit into a bottle and adding the water or alcoholic drink to it. Gin ,vodka etc. Leave it to dissolve into the mix for some days and you can drink. For soups, just throw some of the whole fruit into the boiling soup and leave it to cook together. Take it out of the soup and drink the soup. Very healthy stuff.

author: @alanbuckner5848
text: Love your videos. You advised your viewers to bring a power adapter. Travelers from the USA 🇺🇸 not only need to bring a power adapter but need to bring a power converter as well. Ghana uses 220 voltage for all electrical needs while the USA 🇺🇸 uses 110 voltage to charge our phones, iPads and laptops. Without using a proper power converter you essentially blow out all your devices using 220 volts of electricity on devices made for 110 voltage. Adapter fits your power outlets. Power converters steps down 220 volts of electricity to 110 volts for Americans 🇺🇸 to safely use while in Ghana and Europe as well. Hope this helps. I’m an American man interracially married to my Ghanaian wife 🇪🇹. We have made a few trips to Ghana and other countries and know the importance of power converters and power adapters.

author: @alanbuckner5848
text: May I pass on more information you may wish to inform travelers going to Ghana? Only drink bottled water and only brush your teeth with bottled water. Don’t eat street foods because some vendors don’t practice proper sanitation with handling and storage of food products. Negotiate taxi charges prior to getting in any taxi or have your Ghanaian wife negotiate any charges or use an Uber for transportation. Exchange your 🇺🇸 US $$ at Ghanaian banks for the official exchange rate. The money exchange rate at the Accra Airport pays travelers at a lower unofficial exchange rate. Hope this helps.

author: @garthvanthul
text: You pretty much said this in terms of suggesting having good relations with neighbors (which engender both information sharing and neighbors who *want* to look out for you when you're absent), but I think something that most expats (or at least American expats) don't fully appreciate about living in most of Africa (or any other society where where community norms and solidarity are stronger than modern institutions, like the police) is just how much ALL of your neighbors know about your comings and goings (and those of other people coming to your house--whether friends, staff or service workers). As soon as a house is empty of all human presence, you can safely assume that the entire neighborhood is aware of it, and the risk of theft increases exponentially. Many houses (not just expat) will have a "security guard" who is far too old, fragile and ill-equipped to fend of anyone attempting to enter--hell, he might even sleep through most of the night--but still his presence is making the house safer, because everyone in the neighborhood knows that he is there. And, like the story in this account highlights, as soon as that guard is out sick, everyone will know that as well. That doesn't mean that the information of the missing guard was shared by someone who wanted to help someone else steal your friend's car battery, but when something is common knowledge, it is common knowledge, which can be useful to those few 'bandits' who want to take ill advantage of it.

author: @KwekuTed
text: I'm Ghanaian, I live in the capital city away from the parts shown initially in the video. Those parts are huge slums, situated along the coast (Jamestown, korle and Bukom). They are some of the oldest townships in the Capital, towns that initially sprung up with the arrival of the British (traders of goods and later slaves). These parts used to be called British Accra. The residents are mainly fishermen and traders and sadly place very little priority on education and are consequently caught in cycle of generational poverty, a plight worsened by a poor economy. They however have produced most of the famous boxers that have come out of Ghana, including the hall of famer Azumah Nelson. The other part of the video shows largely non Accra natives, who have moved from other parts of the country to the Capital in search of a better life but have found themselves doing odd jobs and trades and have resorted to living in the slums as the opportunity they had hoped for is highly lacking thanks to the declining economy. It's quite unfortunate but there are no signs that this situation will change for the better any time soon.

author: @BongoBeng1
text: Cape Coast Castle and Elmina Castle are two of the most iconic and historically significant sites in Ghana—and in the world. They deserve global visibility, respectful preservation, and proper digital representation. Sadly, they’ve received far too little of that from the very institution meant to promote them. Let’s be clear: the Ghana Tourism Authority has not done nearly enough to ensure these national landmarks are accessible online to travelers, educators, historians, and the diaspora. The official websites for Cape Coast Castle and Elmina Castle? They don’t exist—not because of budget issues, but because they were never prioritized. The only reason these castles have had an online presence for years is due to private initiative, private funding, and private effort. Individuals—not the Authority—stepped up, paid out of pocket, and kept these important historical sites visible to the world. And yet, when promotion happens, logos and claims are slapped onto campaigns as if the castles stand because of the Authority’s work. That’s simply not true—and it's misleading. If private individuals hadn’t taken responsibility, there would be no websites, no digital outreach, no reliable online information about these UNESCO World Heritage Sites. It’s time that was acknowledged. These castles are not just “tourist attractions”—they are sacred, painful, powerful reminders of history. They deserve more than passive promotion. They deserve an active, professional, and sustained commitment—not just from individuals who care, but from the very institutions entrusted with protecting Ghana’s heritage. Until then, let’s give credit where it’s due. And let’s start demanding more from those in charge.

author: @martyjones1671
text: Despite the claims by Senegal's tour guides and tourism industry, Goree Island was never a major shipping point for slaves, say historians. No slaves were ever sold at what is known as the "House of Slaves." No Africans ever stepped through the famous "door of no return" to waiting ships, either. "The whole story is phony," says Philip D. Curtin, a retired professor of history at the Johns Hopkins University who has written more than two dozen books on Atlantic slave trade and African history. First used as stopover by Portuguese sailors in the 15th century, Goree Island was bought for a few iron nails by the Dutch before being seized by the French and the British. Although it functioned as a commercial center, it was never a key departure point for slaves, Curtin says. Most Africans sold into slavery in the Senegal region would have departed from thriving slave depots at the mouths of the Senegal River to the north and the Gambia River to the south, he says.During about 400 years of the Atlantic slave trade when an estimated 10 million Africans were taken from Africa, maybe 50,000 slaves - not 20 million as claimed by the Slave House curator - might have spent time on the island, Curtin says. Even then, they would not have been locked in chains in the House of Slaves, Curtin says. Built in 1775-1778 by a wealthy merchant, it was one of the most beautiful homes on the island; it would not have been used as a warehouse for slaves other than those who might have been owned by the merchant. Likewise, Curtin adds, the widely accepted story that the "door of no return" was the final departure point for millions of slaves is not true. There are too many rocks to allow boats to dock safely and a beach nearby that would have been the easiest place for loading ships, he says. Curtin's assessment is widely shared by historians, including Abdoulaye Camara, curator of the Goree Island Historical Museum, which is a 10-minute walk from the Slave House.The Slave House, says Camara, offers a distorted account of the island's history - created with tourists in mind....
